title: The battlefield inside
hookLine: a book that opens on a battlefield, read by a man of nonviolence

lines: TWO ARMIES, ONE GAP BETWEEN THEM.
A MAN OF PEACE, A BOOK OF WAR?
cards: Two armies face each other on an open field. Conch shells sound across the lines. A warrior named Arjuna asks his charioteer to drive out into the gap between them.
He looks across and sees teachers, uncles, cousins, old friends. His bow slips from his hand. That's where the Bhagavad Gita begins, weapons about to be loosed.
Gandhi, the man the world knew for nonviolence, kept this book close and called it a guide for his life. How does a man of peace live by a book set on a battlefield?

teach.h: HE READ THE FIELD AS THE HEART.
teach.b: Gandhi made his own version of the Gita in Gujarati and called it Anasakti Yoga. In its introduction he says that he didn't read the war as history. He read the field as the human heart.
The two armies, in his reading, are the forces of good and evil inside one person, and the battle is the one each of us fights there.

Krishna, the charioteer, is for him the dweller within, the voice that speaks from the inside. So when Krishna tells Arjuna to stand up and fight, Gandhi hears: don't run from the struggle inside you.
A text that seems to send a man into battle becomes, in his hands, a handbook for a nonviolent life.
After years of trying to live the Gita's teaching, he wrote, he found its complete selflessness isn't possible without nonviolence.
This is one reading among several.

Other readers, traditional commentators among them, take the war as a real war and Arjuna's duty as a warrior's real duty: Krishna tells a soldier to do what his role asks, without hatred and without clinging to victory.
Still others hold both at once, a real field and a mirror of the inner one. The Gita's first line names the place twice: dharmakshetra, kurukshetra.

teach.h: THE FIELD OF DHARMA, THE FIELD OF THE KURUS.
teach.b: The field of dharma, the field of the Kurus.
Read Gandhi's way, the first name carries the weight: the field of right living is the ground between what a person wants to do and what they know is right.

how: Readers of Gandhi's Anasakti Yoga often read the Gita's battle as a picture of the struggle within, and some Hindus keep a short daily reading of the Gita alongside their prayers.

o: Gandhi's own new scripture, written to replace the Gita
a war history Gandhi studied to plan his campaigns
the Gita read as a battle fought inside the heart

games.q: you're Gandhi, a man committed to nonviolence, and the book you love begins with a god telling a warrior to fight. what do you do with it?
o: put the book aside as a book about war.
read the battlefield as the heart, and the fight as the struggle inside.
take it as a command to go to war.
games.why: in his introduction to Anasakti Yoga, he says he read the field as the heart, and Krishna as the dweller within.

practice: Bring to mind one small battle you're in: something you want to say and suspect you shouldn't, or something you know is right and keep putting off.
Do what Arjuna did, and drive out into the gap to look at both sides calmly, the side that pulls on the in-breath, the side that asks on the out-breath, without choosing yet.
If you pray, you can hold the whole field before Krishna, or before the one you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Gandhi's Gita. The Bhagavad Gita as Gandhi read it: a battle fought inside the heart, with Krishna as the voice within.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: kurukshetra, the field of the Kurus, where the Gita's two armies meet.

carryVoice: Your line: the battle is inside. Tomorrow, the one word Gandhi put on the cover. That's day nine hundred fifty-seven.
